name: Abbey Road
fact: It is nowhere near the Beatles' Abbey Road in Westminster, so signs at the station redirect confused tourists who get off here.

name: Abbey Wood
fact: In the 1860s William Morris regularly travelled from here to his home, the Red House in Bexleyheath, often bringing Arts and Crafts guests.

name: Acton Central
fact: Trains change power source here, swapping from overhead wires at 25,000 volts to a third rail carrying 750 volts.

name: Acton Main Line
fact: It served a garden estate built by the Great Western Railway in the 1920s to house its own staff, mostly drivers from Old Oak Common depot.

name: Acton Town
fact: It was called Mill Hill Park until 1910, and its Grade II listed building is Charles Holden's brick, concrete and glass design of 1932.

name: Aldgate
fact: The station sits on a plague pit behind St Botolph's church thought to hold around 1,000 bodies.

name: Aldgate East
fact: In 1938 the whole station was shifted east and 1,400 feet of track lowered, with the line staying open for most of the work.

name: All Saints
fact: It takes its name from the parish church of All Saints, built in the 1820s, and announcements add "for Chrisp Street Market".

name: Alperton
fact: It opened in 1903 under the name Perivale-Alperton, and was rebuilt in the 1930s to a Charles Holden design.

name: Amersham
fact: At 147 metres above sea level it is the highest station on the Underground, standing taller than the Big Ben tower.

name: Anerley
fact: The name is said to come from a Scottish landowner calling his home the "annerly hoose", the only house in what was then open country.

name: Angel
fact: Its escalators rise 27 metres over a length of 61 metres, the longest on the Underground and in the United Kingdom.

name: Archway
fact: It opened in 1907 as Highgate, and only took the name Archway for good in 1947 once a new Highgate station had been built up the hill.

name: Arnos Grove
fact: Charles Holden's drum-shaped ticket hall is Grade II* listed and was said to be inspired by Stockholm City Library.

name: Arsenal
fact: It is the only tube station named directly after a football club, renamed from Gillespie Road in 1932 after lobbying by manager Herbert Chapman.

name: Baker Street
fact: With ten platforms it has more than any other Underground station, and two of them survive from the line's opening in 1863.

name: Balham
fact: A bomb fell on the road above the platform tunnels on 14 October 1940, killing sixty-six people sheltering below.

name: Bank
fact: The Bank and Monument complex has 31 escalators and four moving walkways, more than any other station on the Underground.

name: Barbican
fact: It stands on the site of a house in Aldersgate Street that for years carried a sign claiming "This was Shakespeare's House".

name: Barking
fact: Its 1961 concrete and glass booking hall, by British Railways architects led by John Ward, has been Grade II listed since 1995.

name: Barking Riverside
fact: It opened in 2022 on the site of the old Barking Power Station, built because 10,800 planned homes could not go ahead without it.

name: Barkingside
fact: The Grade II listed station has a cupola on its roof and a hammerbeam ceiling in the ticket hall, more country church than tube stop.

name: Barons Court
fact: Its wooden platform benches, with the station name spelled out on enamel panels along the back, are unique on the Underground.

name: Battersea Power Station
fact: It opened in September 2021, the first major extension of the Underground since the Jubilee line was extended in 1999.

name: Bayswater
fact: Near the station, 23 and 24 Leinster Gardens are fake house fronts with blank windows, put up to hide the railway cutting behind them.

name: Beckton
fact: Beckton is named after Simon Adams Beck, the gas company governor in charge when work on the vast Beckton Gas Works began in 1868.

name: Beckton Park
fact: Tucked in a cutting under a roundabout, it is the least used station on the whole DLR network.

name: Becontree
fact: It opened as Gale Street Halt in 1926 to serve a new estate that by 1935 held about 18,000 homes and 116,000 people.

name: Belsize Park
fact: It is one of eight Underground stations with a deep-level air-raid shelter dug beneath it during the Second World War.

name: Bermondsey
fact: Ian Ritchie's design uses latticed concrete beams so that daylight from the street reaches down to the platforms.

name: Bethnal Green
fact: In March 1943, years before it opened as a station, 173 people died in a crush on the stairs down to the shelter below.

name: Blackfriars
fact: It is the only London station whose platforms span the Thames, and its roof of 4,400 solar panels made it the world's largest solar bridge.

name: Blackhorse Road
fact: A fibreglass relief of a shying black horse on blue mosaic, by sculptor David McFall, has fronted the station since it opened in 1968.

name: Blackwall
fact: It sits beside the northern entrance to the Blackwall Tunnel; the original Blackwall station stood further east, on what is now Jamestown Way.

name: Bond Street
fact: The railway's original plans called it Davies Street, and the Elizabeth line platforms opened five months late after tunnelling problems.

name: Borough
fact: It opened in 1890 on the City and South London Railway, the world's first successful deep-level tube.

name: Boston Manor
fact: Its Grade II listed tower carries a vertical strip of glass bricks that lights up after dark, a 1930s Art Deco beacon over the tracks.

name: Bounds Green
fact: A single bomb dropped on houses nearby on 13 October 1940 collapsed one of the platform tunnels onto people sheltering below.

name: Bow Church
fact: It is named after the 14th-century Bow Church, and its tracks follow a railway route first opened in 1852.

name: Bow Road
fact: The Grade II listed station opened in temporary buildings in 1902, and east of it the tracks climb steeply at 1 in 40.

name: Brent Cross
fact: It opened in 1923 simply as Brent, after the river, and was renamed in 1976 on the day the shopping centre opened.

name: Brentwood
fact: It opened in 1840 as the temporary end of the line from London, with trains going no further east until 1843.

name: Brixton
fact: The tiled murals in the platform seat recesses, by Hans Unger, show a ton of bricks as a pun on the station's name.

name: Brockley
fact: The name is thought to mean a woodland clearing where badgers were seen, from broc, the Old English for badger.

name: Bromley-by-Bow
fact: It was plain Bromley from 1858 until 1967, when "by-Bow" was added to stop people confusing it with Bromley in Kent.

name: Brondesbury
fact: It opened in 1860 as Edgeware Road (Kilburn) and went through four more names before settling on Brondesbury in 1883.

name: Brondesbury Park
fact: Brondesbury almost certainly takes its name from a man called Brand, who appears in documents about the manor from around 1192.

name: Bruce Grove
fact: It is named after nearby Bruce Castle, in turn named after Robert the Bruce, whose English lands here were seized by Edward I.

name: Buckhurst Hill
fact: It opened in 1856 as a country railway station and only joined the Underground in 1948, when the branch became part of the Central line.

name: Burnham
fact: It opened in 1899 under the name Burnham Beeches, after the ancient woodland nearby, and only became plain Burnham in 1975.

name: Burnt Oak
fact: It was nearly called Sheves Hill, a name that actually made it onto a printed Underground map in 1924.

name: Bush Hill Park
fact: The station opened in 1880 on farmland belonging to Bush Hill Park House, and the first streets of the suburb went up within six years.

name: Bushey
fact: Bakerloo line trains from central London called here until 1982, when the Underground service was cut back.

name: Caledonian Road
fact: Its lifts drop straight to platform level with no stairs in between, unusual for its age and the reason it is step-free today.

name: Caledonian Road & Barnsbury
fact: It opened in 1870 as Barnsbury, replacing an earlier Caledonian Road station just to the west, and gained its double name in 1893.

name: Cambridge Heath
fact: Although it opened in 1872, it had no daytime trains at all until 1998 and none in the evenings or at weekends until 2001.

name: Camden Road
fact: Its Venetian Gothic building of 1870, in yellow Suffolk brick, is the last station by architect Edwin Henry Horne still used as a station.

name: Camden Town
fact: Until 2019 it was exit-only on Sundays, because crowds heading for Camden Market made the narrow passages unsafe.

name: Canada Water
fact: Its glass drum, 25 metres across, drops daylight all the way down to the Jubilee line platforms 22 metres below the street.

name: Canary Wharf
fact: Norman Foster's station sits in a drained arm of the old West India Docks, in a pit 24 metres deep and 265 metres long.

name: Canning Town
fact: The DLR platforms sit directly on top of the Jubilee line platforms, so changing lines means only walking up or down one flight.

name: Cannon Street
fact: The station was shut every Sunday from 1918 until January 2015, a gap of almost a century.

name: Canonbury
fact: It opened in 1858 under the name Newington Road and Balls Pond Road, becoming Canonbury only in 1870.

name: Canons Park
fact: With about 1.68 million passengers a year, it is the least used station on the Jubilee line.

name: Carpenders Park
fact: Opened in 1914 to serve a nearby golf course, and replaced in 1952 by the present station 210 metres to the south.

name: Chadwell Heath
fact: It stands on the site of Wangey House, one of Dagenham's oldest buildings, parts of which dated back to 1250.

name: Chalfont & Latimer
fact: It opened in 1889 as Chalfont Road, taking its double-barrelled name in 1915, and is the junction for the Chesham branch.

name: Chalk Farm
fact: Its wedge-shaped building has the longest frontage of any Leslie Green station, and its lift shafts, at 21 feet, are the shallowest on the network.

name: Chancery Lane
fact: The deep-level air-raid shelter beneath it was turned after the war into the Kingsway telephone exchange.

name: Charing Cross
fact: Its closed Jubilee line platforms are kept in working order and hired out for filming, appearing in Skyfall, Thor and Paddington.

name: Chesham
fact: The 3.89-mile gap between Chesham and Chalfont & Latimer is the longest between two adjacent stations anywhere on the Underground.

name: Cheshunt
fact: During the 2012 Olympics, Cheshunt was one of the main rail gateways to the canoe events at the Lee Valley White Water Centre.

name: Chigwell
fact: The station appears in Mike Leigh's 1983 film Meantime.

name: Chingford
fact: The station stands close to Queen Elizabeth's Hunting Lodge, and was moved to its present site in 1878, five years after it opened.

name: Chiswick Park
fact: Piccadilly line trains rush straight through, because the platforms only reach the outer District line tracks.

name: Chorleywood
fact: A Grade II listed K8 telephone kiosk still stands on Platform 2, now wired into TfL's internal phone system.

name: Clapham Common
fact: One of only two underground stations left with a narrow island platform, about 3.7 metres wide with trains on both sides.

name: Clapham High Street
fact: The station building on the eastbound platform was destroyed by a bomb in 1944.

name: Clapham Junction
fact: It is not in Clapham at all, and it is the busiest station in Europe by number of trains, with up to 180 an hour.

name: Clapham North
fact: It opened as Clapham Road in 1900 and was renamed Clapham North in 1926, when the line was extended to Morden.

name: Clapham South
fact: In 1948 many passengers arriving on the Empire Windrush were housed temporarily in the deep-level air-raid shelter beneath the station.

name: Clapton
fact: Greater Anglia trains pass through Clapton every day, but none of them are scheduled to stop.

name: Cockfosters
fact: Platforms 2 and 3 face the same centre track from opposite sides, an arrangement railways call the Spanish solution.

name: Colindale
fact: T. E. Lawrence used this station while posted at Hendon Aerodrome and borrowed its name for his pen name, Colin Dale.

name: Colliers Wood
fact: The pub across the road is called The Charles Holden, after the architect who designed the station.

name: Covent Garden
fact: The 260-metre run to Leicester Square is the shortest distance between any two adjacent stations on the network.

name: Crossharbour
fact: It was called Crossharbour & London Arena from 1994 until the arena was demolished in 2006.

name: Crouch Hill
fact: The station opened in 1868 and sits 3.8 miles from St Pancras.

name: Croxley
fact: It opened as Croxley Green in 1925 and was shortened to Croxley in 1949 to stop it being confused with another Croxley Green station.

name: Crystal Palace
fact: The tunnel beside the station was cut through clay directly beneath one of the Crystal Palace's great water towers.

name: Custom House
fact: The DLR station closed for almost a year from February 2017 while it was rebuilt to make room for the Elizabeth line.

name: Cutty Sark
fact: One of only four fully underground DLR stations, 20 metres down, where three-car trains open only their middle doors.

name: Cyprus
fact: The station sits in a cutting beneath an elevated roundabout, in an area named after the Mediterranean island of Cyprus.

name: Dagenham East
fact: It opened simply as Dagenham in 1885 and only gained the East in its name in 1949.

name: Dagenham Heathway
fact: The station front lost its symmetry in the 1970s when 50 feet of the building was demolished to fit in a neighbouring one.

name: Dalston Junction
fact: Closed in 1986, the station stood shut for 24 years until the Mayor of London reopened it in 2010.

name: Dalston Kingsland
fact: The station closed in 1865 and did not reopen for another 118 years, returning as Dalston Kingsland in 1983.

name: Debden
fact: Two new lifts made Debden the 82nd step-free station on the Underground in April 2021.

name: Denmark Hill
fact: In the 1920s the waiting room housed the Mystical Church of the Comforter, where babies were baptised and one marriage was held.

name: Deptford Bridge
fact: The platforms are carried on a viaduct high above the road and Deptford Creek.

name: Devons Road
fact: One of the few DLR stations to keep its original look, with half-cylindrical glazed blue canopies over the platforms.

name: Dollis Hill
fact: The station has changed lines twice, opening on the Metropolitan in 1909, moving to the Bakerloo in 1939 and the Jubilee in 1979.

name: Ealing Broadway
fact: The station opened in December 1838, months after Brunel's Great Western Railway first ran broad gauge trains through Ealing.

name: Ealing Common
fact: Charles Holden gave the station a seven-sided ticket hall in Portland stone, glazed on every side.

name: Earl's Court
fact: The Underground's first escalators opened here on 4 October 1911, with a one-legged man known as Bumper Harris riding them to reassure the public.

name: East Acton
fact: Two extra freight tracks beside the station opened in 1938 and closed in 1964, and their overgrown trackbed is still visible.

name: East Finchley
fact: The tunnel running from here to Morden was, when it opened, the longest railway tunnel in the world at 17.25 miles.

name: East Ham
fact: The Edwardian brick station building, rebuilt in 1902, has been Grade II listed since 1999.

name: East India
fact: The Greenwich Prime Meridian crosses the tracks at the end of the platforms, marked by an illuminated blue line at street level.

name: East Putney
fact: British Rail sold the line through the station to London Underground in 1994 for the nominal sum of one pound.

name: Eastcote
fact: It opened in 1906 as Eastcote Halt, and Charles Holden later replaced it with a cube-shaped ticket hall of brick and glass.

name: Edgware
fact: The line was meant to carry on north-west to Bushey Heath, but the plan died when the Green Belt stopped the housing it would have served.

name: Edgware Road (Bakerloo)
fact: London Transport proposed closing the station in 1983 rather than pay to replace its 77-year-old lifts, and was overruled.

name: Edgware Road (Circle)
fact: One of the original stops on the world's first underground railway, open since 10 January 1863.

name: Edmonton Green
fact: The station was called Lower Edmonton (High Level) for more than a century, taking its present name only in 1992.

name: Elephant & Castle
fact: A girl born here on 13 May 1924 was the first baby born on the Underground network.

name: Elm Park
fact: Built by a housing developer in 1935, it was the last station squeezed into an existing Underground line until Wood Lane in 2008.

name: Elverson Road
fact: The station straddles a borough boundary, so crossing the footbridge to the other platform means stepping from Lewisham into Greenwich.

name: Embankment
fact: The northbound Northern line platform is the only place still using Oswald Laurence's Mind the Gap recording, restored in 2013 at his widow's request.

name: Emerson Park
fact: The only stop between Romford and Upminster, and the least used London Overground station on the network.

name: Enfield Town
fact: Open since 1849, the station only appeared on the Tube map in 2015, when its line was handed to London Overground.

name: Epping
fact: The single-track branch that ran on from Epping to Ongar was the last part of the Underground worked by steam.

name: Euston
fact: Clearing the site for HS2 meant moving about 60,000 graves from the burial ground next door, the largest exhumation in British history.

name: Euston Square
fact: It opened in 1863 as Gower Street and kept that name for 46 years before becoming Euston Square in 1909.

name: Fairlop
fact: The platform canopies still carry the old Great Eastern Railway's symbol in their ironwork.

name: Farringdon
fact: The only station in the country served by both the north-south Thameslink route and the east-west Elizabeth line.

name: Finchley Central
fact: The New Vaudeville Band reached number 11 in 1967 with Finchley Central, a song about waiting on the platform for someone who never arrives.

name: Finchley Road
fact: Metropolitan line trains use the outer platforms and Jubilee line trains the inner pair, all four in the same cutting.

name: Finchley Road & Frognal
fact: The station opened in 1860 under the considerably longer name Finchley Road St Johns Wood.

name: Finsbury Park
fact: The Victoria line platforms are decorated with duelling pistols, thanks to a mix-up with Finsbury Fields three miles away.

name: Forest Gate
fact: The station was shut down in 1843 and only reopened in 1846 after local residents pressed the railway to bring it back.

name: Forest Hill
fact: It opened in 1839 as Dartmouth Arms, named after the local inn, and became Forest Hill in 1845.

name: Fulham Broadway
fact: The 1905 entrance was built by Harry W Ford specifically to cope with crowds heading for the new Stamford Bridge stadium.

name: Gallions Reach
fact: The station is named after Gallions Reach, a stretch of the Thames, rather than after anywhere on dry land.

name: Gants Hill
fact: Its barrel-vaulted concourse was modelled on the Moscow Metro, and it is the only Charles Holden station with no building at street level.

name: Gidea Park
fact: It opened in 1910 as Squirrels Heath & Gidea Park, swapped the two halves round in 1913, and dropped the squirrels in 1969.

name: Gloucester Road
fact: A disused platform here is used as a gallery for Art on the Underground, showing work by artists including David Shrigley.

name: Golders Green
fact: In the tunnels south of the station lies North End, or Bull & Bush, a station that was partly built and never finished.

name: Goldhawk Road
fact: Trains ran past this spot for 50 years before anyone built a station here, in 1914.

name: Goodge Street
fact: From 1943 the deep-level shelter beneath the station was used by the Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force.

name: Goodmayes
fact: Its goods yard once connected to the Becontree Estate Railway, a temporary line laid to carry building materials for the vast Becontree housing estate.

name: Gospel Oak
fact: The platforms for the Barking line closed in 1926 and stayed shut for 55 years, only reopening in 1981.

name: Grange Hill
fact: The original 1903 station building was destroyed by a German V1 flying bomb in July 1944 and had to be rebuilt.

name: Great Portland Street
fact: It opened in 1863 as Portland Road on the world's first underground railway, and from 1923 to 1933 was called Great Portland Street and Regents Park.

name: Green Park
fact: The station was called Dover Street until 1933, when a new ticket hall moved the entrance and it was renamed after the park above.

name: Greenford
fact: It kept the last wooden-treaded escalator on the Underground until 2014, and had the first escalator carrying passengers up to platforms above street level.

name: Greenwich
fact: The station building dates from 1840 and is one of the oldest surviving railway station buildings anywhere in the world.

name: Gunnersbury
fact: The station opened in 1869 under the name Brentford Road and was renamed Gunnersbury two years later.

name: Hackney Central
fact: The station closed in 1944 and did not reopen for 36 years; its original 1870 building is now a bar and music venue.

name: Hackney Downs
fact: It opened in 1872 under the name Hackney Downs Junction, which it kept until 1896.

name: Hackney Wick
fact: Opened only in 1980, the station was rebuilt in 2018 with a subway that doubles as a public cycle and foot route between Hackney and Tower Hamlets.

name: Haggerston
fact: The station closed in May 1940 and its building was bombed months later; it did not reopen for 70 years, until 2010.

name: Hainault
fact: Its lifts are the shallowest on the London Underground, dropping just 18 inches between levels.

name: Hammersmith (District & Piccadilly)
fact: The platforms sit in a cutting directly below Hammersmith bus station, with cross-platform changes between the District and Piccadilly lines.

name: Hammersmith (H&C & Circle)
fact: This is the second station on the site: the original of 1864 stood slightly to the north and was replaced by the present one in 1868.

name: Hampstead
fact: Its platforms are the deepest on the Underground at 58.5 metres below ground, reached by the network's deepest lift shaft.

name: Hampstead Heath
fact: In the nineteenth century as many as 100,000 people a day used the station at weekends and on public holidays, heading for the Heath.

name: Hanger Lane
fact: The roof of its ticket hall forms the centre of the Hanger Lane Gyratory, where the A40 crosses the North Circular.

name: Hanwell
fact: Between 1883 and 1885 District Railway trains called here on their way from Mansion House to Windsor, before the service was dropped as uneconomic.

name: Harlesden
fact: An earlier station called Willesden stood on this site from 1841 until 1866; the present Harlesden opened in 1912.

name: Harold Wood
fact: The name appears as Horalds Wood around 1237 and comes from King Harold Godwinson, defeated by William the Conqueror in 1066.

name: Harringay Green Lanes
fact: The station has carried six names since 1880, among them Harringay Stadium, and was given very long platforms for the crowds heading to the arena.

name: Harrow & Wealdstone
fact: The worst peacetime rail disaster in British history happened here on 8 October 1952, when 112 people were killed and 340 injured.

name: Harrow-on-the-Hill
fact: The station is not on Harrow Hill but at the foot of it, in what was a small hamlet called Greenhill when it opened.

name: Hatch End
fact: The present station was built in 1911 to a design by Gerald Horsley, son of the painter John Callcott Horsley.

name: Hatton Cross
fact: The platform tiling is patterned after the British Airways Speedbird logo, designed by Theyre Lee-Elliott in 1932.

name: Hayes & Harlington
fact: The film Trains at Hayes Station, shot from a factory roof beside the platforms, was among the first demonstrations of stereophonic sound with moving pictures.

name: Headstone Lane
fact: Bakerloo line trains served this station for 65 years, from 1917 until they were withdrawn in September 1982.

name: Heathrow Terminal 4
fact: It is the only station on the Underground where trains run one way only, arriving at its single platform round a loop.

name: Heathrow Terminal 5
fact: Though the station is underground, translucent ETFE panels in the roof let daylight reach both ends of all six platforms.

name: Heathrow Terminals 2 & 3
fact: Queen Elizabeth II opened the station in 1977 under the name Heathrow Central; it has been renamed three times since, most recently in 2016.

name: Hendon Central
fact: Its Grade II listed neo-Georgian entrance, with a Doric colonnade, was designed by Stanley Heaps as the centrepiece of a whole new suburban town.

name: Heron Quays
fact: The station was rebuilt in 2002 inside a new Canary Wharf office tower, with an interior designed by Alsop Architects.

name: High Barnet
fact: A bell cast in 1869 was rung for departing steam trains here until it was handed to Barnet Museum in 1940.

name: High Street Kensington
fact: Platform 3 has one of the few surviving K8 telephone kiosks in Britain, which is Grade II listed.

name: Highams Park
fact: The station opened in 1873 as Hale End and did not settle on the name Highams Park until 1969.

name: Highbury & Islington
fact: A V-1 flying bomb hit the station in June 1944; its 1850 building survived that, only to be demolished in the 1960s for the Victoria line.

name: Highgate
fact: Overgrown surface platforms still stand beside the tube station; they last saw a train in 1954 and the track was lifted by 1972.

name: Hillingdon
fact: The old station was demolished so the A40 could be widened, and its 1990s replacement won a Civic Trust Award for its deconstructivist design.

name: Holborn
fact: Tunnels on the closed Aldwych branch here sheltered treasures from the British Museum during the war, including the Elgin Marbles.

name: Holland Park
fact: The station was given a flat roof in 1900 in the hope that a building would go up on top, as at Queensway, but nothing ever has.

name: Holloway Road
fact: A spiral escalator built here by Jesse W. Reno never carried a passenger; parts of it were later dug out and kept by the London Transport Museum.

name: Homerton
fact: The station closed during the war in 1944 and stayed shut for 40 years, reopening only in May 1985.

name: Honor Oak Park
fact: The housebuilders developing the area put £1,000 towards the cost of building the station, and it was named to distinguish it from nearby Honor Oak.

name: Hornchurch
fact: The station was rebuilt in 1932 by the LMS architect William Henry Hamlyn, in a style borrowed from London Underground stations of the day.

name: Hounslow Central
fact: It opened in 1886 as Heston & Hounslow and was renamed in 1925, on the same day as Hounslow East and Hounslow West.

name: Hounslow East
fact: Staff play classical music over the public address system as an experiment to discourage anti-social behaviour at the station.

name: Hounslow West
fact: Charles Holden's 1931 ticket hall is seven-sided, a theme carried through to a chandelier with seven lamps.

name: Hoxton
fact: The First World War memorial at the entrance came from the closed Broad Street station by way of Richmond, returning near its original home in 2011.

name: Hyde Park Corner
fact: Leslie Green's ox-blood tiled station building was left behind when escalators replaced the lifts in 1932, and is now part of the Wellesley Hotel.

name: Ickenham
fact: When the halt opened, villagers living nearby sold flowers from their gardens and served teas to Londoners out for a day in the country.

name: Ilford
fact: The station once handled 200,000 milk churns, and a bridge fitted with lifts down to platform level was built to move them.

name: Imperial Wharf
fact: One of London's newest stations, it opened in 2009 to serve a former industrial riverside site rebuilt as 1,800 flats.

name: Island Gardens
fact: In March 1987, before the DLR opened, a test train crashed through the buffers and was left hanging from the end of the elevated track here.

name: Iver
fact: Trains had been passing the spot for 86 years before a station appeared: the line opened in 1838, but Iver station only in 1924.

name: Kennington
fact: Its T. P. Figgis building is the only station of the original City & South London Railway still close to its first design, and the only listed one.

name: Kensal Green
fact: In October 1986 a British Rail train ran into the back of an Underground train at the station, injuring 23 people.

name: Kensal Rise
fact: The station opened in 1873 under the name Kensal Green and was only renamed Kensal Rise in 1890.

name: Kensington (Olympia)
fact: Bombed in the Second World War and closed, it reopened in 1946 and later served as a terminus for Motorail car-carrying trains.

name: Kentish Town
fact: The tube station shut in June 2023 so its two escalators could be replaced, and did not reopen until December 2024, six months late.

name: Kentish Town West
fact: A fire closed the station in April 1971 and it stayed shut for more than ten years, reopening in October 1981.

name: Kenton
fact: The station's old coal yard, no longer needed by the railway, is now the site of a Sainsbury's supermarket.

name: Kew Gardens
fact: It is the only station on the Underground with a pub attached, once reached by a door leading straight onto platform 1.

name: Kilburn
fact: A viaduct just beyond the platforms still carries the words METROPOLITAN RAILWAY and the date 1914 along its sides.

name: Kilburn High Road
fact: Its street-level buildings and footbridge are the result not of modernisation but of three or four major fires since the early 1970s.

name: Kilburn Park
fact: Designed by Stanley Heaps, it was one of the first Underground stations built specifically to use escalators rather than lifts.

name: King George V
fact: Named after the dock beside it, the station was the end of the line until 2009, when the DLR was extended under the Thames to Woolwich Arsenal.

name: King's Cross St. Pancras
fact: The 1987 fire that killed 31 people here revealed a previously unknown effect, since called the trench effect, that sends flames racing up escalators.

name: Kingsbury
fact: The name is something of a fiction: the station stands in the eastern edge of Kenton, and Kingsbury proper is closer to Neasden.

name: Knightsbridge
fact: The station only became step-free in April 2025, more than a century after it opened, when a new entrance was built.

name: Ladbroke Grove
fact: It opened in 1864 as Notting Hill, and was renamed to stop passengers confusing it with the newer Notting Hill Gate.

name: Lambeth North
fact: A German bomb in January 1941 wrecked the southbound platform tunnel, injuring 28 people who were sheltering there.

name: Lancaster Gate
fact: Despite the name, the station sits about 300 metres east of the Lancaster Gate entrance to Kensington Gardens.

name: Langdon Park
fact: An infill station slotted into an existing stretch of railway, it cost £10.5 million and opened in December 2007.

name: Langley
fact: Trains ran through Langley on Brunel's Great Western main line from 1838, but the village waited until 1845 for a station.

name: Latimer Road
fact: The station stands roughly 500 metres from Latimer Road itself, which was named after the Elizabethan benefactor Edward Latymer.

name: Leicester Square
fact: Film sprocket holes are painted along all four platforms, a nod to the premiere cinemas in the square above.

name: Lewisham
fact: Platform 3 keeps its original canopy, held up by cast iron brackets decorated with cherries.

name: Leyton
fact: The station opened under the name Low Leyton, becoming plain Leyton in 1867.

name: Leyton Midland Road
fact: It opened in 1894 simply as Leyton, and only gained the Midland Road part of its name in 1949.

name: Leytonstone
fact: Mosaics of Alfred Hitchcock's life and films line the station, commissioned for the centenary of the director's birth nearby.

name: Leytonstone High Road
fact: Goods wagons were once lowered from the raised railway arches to the yard below by hydraulic hoist.

name: Limehouse
fact: The Great Storm of 1987 destroyed the station's roof and canopy.

name: Liverpool Street
fact: The station was built on a ten-acre site previously occupied by the Bethlem Royal Hospital, the asylum known as Bedlam.

name: London Bridge
fact: Opened in 1836, it is the oldest railway station in London's zone 1 and one of the oldest anywhere in the world.

name: London City Airport
fact: Drew Primary School, a century-old building with classrooms on its roof, stood on the site before the station was built.

name: London Fields
fact: A fire in 1981 badly damaged the station buildings and services stopped for five years before it reopened in 1986.

name: Loughton
fact: The Grade II listed station, designed by John Murray Easton, has sweeping gull-winged concrete canopies over its platforms.

name: Maida Vale
fact: When it opened in 1915 it was the first station on the Underground to be staffed entirely by women.

name: Maidenhead
fact: A bronze statue on platform 3 honours Sir Nicholas Winton, who brought 669 children out of Prague in 1939.

name: Manor House
fact: Charles Holden gave the station nine street-level entrances, two of them built to feed passengers straight onto the trams.

name: Manor Park
fact: The station opened in 1873 under the longer name Manor Park and Little Ilford.

name: Mansion House
fact: Britain's first penny chocolate vending machine was installed here in July 1886.

name: Marble Arch
fact: The plain white platform tiles were replaced in 1985 by enamel panels designed by the artist Annabel Grey.

name: Maryland
fact: It opened in 1873 as Maryland Point and lost the Point from its name in 1940.

name: Marylebone
fact: Several scenes of the Beatles' film A Hard Day's Night were shot here in April 1964.

name: Mile End
fact: In 2007 a Central line train was derailed here after hitting a roll of fire blanket blown out of a cross-passage between the tunnels.

name: Mill Hill East
fact: It is the only station on a single-track branch of the Northern line, extended there to serve the army's Inglis Barracks.

name: Monument
fact: The station opened as Eastcheap in October 1884 and was renamed The Monument less than a month later.

name: Moor Park
fact: The station was originally called Sandy Lodge, after the golf course it was built to serve.

name: Moorgate
fact: The 1975 crash here, in which a train ran at speed into a dead-end tunnel, killed 43 people and remains the Underground's worst peacetime accident.

name: Morden
fact: This is the most southerly station on the whole Underground network.

name: Mornington Crescent
fact: Closed in 1992 to replace its lifts, it stayed shut for six years, reopening after a campaign helped along by the Radio 4 game named after it.

name: Mudchute
fact: It was going to be called Millwall Park, but locals feared away fans would arrive here and find the ground was across the river.

name: Neasden
fact: The station opened in 1880 under the name Kingsbury and Neasden, dropping Kingsbury only in 1932.

name: New Cross
fact: A fire that started in a paint shop in October 1844 destroyed the carriage sheds, engine sheds and workshops beside the station.

name: New Cross Gate
fact: For a few months in 1847 this was the northern terminus of an experimental atmospheric railway, which moved trains without locomotives.

name: Newbury Park
fact: Its copper barrel-vaulted bus station, designed by Oliver Hill, won a Festival of Britain award in 1951 and is Grade II listed.

name: Nine Elms
fact: Opened in 2021, it was part of the first major extension of the Underground since the Jubilee line reached Stratford in 1999.

name: North Acton
fact: A third platform was added in 1992 so trains can turn back here when there is trouble elsewhere on the Central line.

name: North Ealing
fact: It was the only station on its branch not rebuilt in the 1930s, so it keeps its original Edwardian, faintly rural look.

name: North Greenwich
fact: The deep blue tiles lining the cavernous interior were inspired by the colour-coded stations of the Hong Kong metro.

name: North Harrow
fact: Trains had been running past this spot for 30 years before a station finally opened here in 1915.

name: North Wembley
fact: The station was going to be called East Lane, after the road crossing the railway, but opened in 1912 as North Wembley.

name: Northfields
fact: It opened in 1908 as Northfield (Ealing) and spent two decades under the name Northfields and Little Ealing.

name: Northolt
fact: A Great Western Railway halt stood just east of here from 1907 until the Central line arrived in 1948 and replaced it.

name: Northwick Park
fact: The island platform holds one of the few surviving K8 telephone kiosks, which is Grade II listed in its own right.

name: Northwood
fact: Two Metropolitan line trains collided in fog just outside the station on New Year's Eve 1945, killing three people.

name: Northwood Hills
fact: The station's name was picked in a competition, won by a woman from North Harrow before it opened in 1933.

name: Norwood Junction
fact: The world's first railway flyover was built just south of the station, carrying an experimental atmospheric line over the steam railway.

name: Notting Hill Gate
fact: Refurbishment in 2010 uncovered a lift passage sealed up since 1959, its walls still covered in posters from the late 1950s.

name: Oakwood
fact: The station opened in 1933 as Enfield West and did not take the name Oakwood until 1946.

name: Old Street
fact: The old surface building was swept away in 1968 and replaced by a ticket hall sunk into the middle of the roundabout.

name: Osterley
fact: A brick tower topped with a concrete obelisk marks the station, said to be inspired by a building Charles Holden saw in Amsterdam.

name: Oval
fact: In 2004 staff here began chalking a daily thought from the Tao Te Ching on a whiteboard, and the habit spread to other stations.

name: Oxford Circus
fact: While the Victoria line was dug beneath it, traffic crossed the junction for five and a half years on a temporary steel deck nicknamed the umbrella.

name: Paddington
fact: Paddington Bear is named after the station, and a statue of him sits under the clock on platform 1.

name: Park Royal
fact: The name comes from the Royal Agricultural Society's Park Royal show grounds, which the first station here was built to serve.

name: Parsons Green
fact: The District Railway reached Parsons Green in 1880, with the station designed under the supervision of the engineer John Wolfe Barry.

name: Peckham Rye
fact: A Victorian waiting room above the concourse was bricked up for 55 years before being rediscovered and partly restored.

name: Penge West
fact: The first station here closed in 1841 for want of passengers, reopening in 1863 once crowds began heading for the Crystal Palace.

name: Perivale
fact: Designed in 1938, the station was held up by the Second World War and opened in 1947 without the tower its architect had planned.

name: Piccadilly Circus
fact: The Eros statue overhead was carted off to Victoria Embankment Gardens while the circular ticket hall was dug out beneath it.

name: Pimlico
fact: It is the only station on the Victoria line with no interchange to any other Underground or National Rail line.

name: Pinner
fact: Houses built here during the Metro-land boom had to be worth at least £1,000, a higher bar than at Harrow-on-the-Hill.

name: Plaistow
fact: The station opened in 1858 on a new short cut the London, Tilbury and Southend Railway built from Fenchurch Street to Barking.

name: Pontoon Dock
fact: Opened in 2005, the station stands high enough to give views south across Thames Barrier Park to the Thames Barrier.

name: Poplar
fact: A third station called Poplar was built nearby in 1851 but never opened to passengers.

name: Preston Road
fact: It opened in 1908 as a halt serving the clay pigeon shooting events of that year's Olympic Games.

name: Prince Regent
fact: The station is named after Prince Regent Lane, laid out in 1811 and named for the man who became George IV.

name: Pudding Mill Lane
fact: Despite sitting right beside the Olympic Park, the station was closed throughout the 2012 Games because it was far too small for the crowds.

name: Putney Bridge
fact: Despite the name, the station is on the Fulham side of the Thames and is not actually in Putney.

name: Queen's Park
fact: The station opened in 1879 as Queen's Park (West Kilburn), and Bakerloo line trains did not reach it until 1915.

name: Queens Road Peckham
fact: Passenger trains to the East London line stopped running in 1911, and the link was not restored until London Overground reinstated it in 2012.

name: Queensbury
fact: The name Queensbury was invented when the station opened in 1934, coined simply to match neighbouring Kingsbury.

name: Queensway
fact: Renamed from Queen's Road in 1946, the station keeps its 1900 building, given a flat roof so shops and offices could be built on top.

name: Ravenscourt Park
fact: The station opened in 1873 as Shaftesbury Road and was renamed in 1888, just before the nearby park opened to the public.

name: Rayners Lane
fact: Named after a local farmer, Daniel Rayner, the exposed halt here was once nicknamed Pneumonia Junction.

name: Reading
fact: Opened in 1840 as the temporary western terminus of the Great Western Railway, the station was rebuilt for £897 million and reopened in 2014.

name: Rectory Road
fact: The ticket office, street buildings, staircases and platform shelters all date from mid-1980s works funded by the Greater London Council.

name: Redbridge
fact: The tunnels here were used by the Plessey company as an aircraft parts factory from 1942 to 1945, before the station ever opened to passengers.

name: Regent's Park
fact: The station has no building at street level at all, and is reached only by a subway from the pavement.

name: Richmond
fact: The Art Deco station building dates from 1937 and was designed by Southern Railway's chief architect James Robb Scott, in Portland stone.

name: Rickmansworth
fact: From 1925 this was the point where Metropolitan line trains swapped their electric locomotive for a steam one to continue north.

name: Roding Valley
fact: It is the least used station on the London Underground, with around 170,000 passenger journeys in 2024.

name: Romford
fact: The Upminster branch had its own separate station at Romford until 1934, because the Great Eastern Railway refused to share.

name: Rotherhithe
fact: The platforms sit at the southern end of the Brunels' 1843 Thames Tunnel, and its original brickwork is visible from the platform end.

name: Royal Albert
fact: It stands further from the nearest houses than any other station on the DLR.

name: Royal Oak
fact: The station is named after a nearby pub, The Royal Oak, which has since been renamed The Porchester.

name: Royal Victoria
fact: The line through the station dates from 1855, when the Eastern Counties Railway was forced to divert around the newly opened Royal Victoria Dock.

name: Ruislip
fact: When the line from Harrow-on-the-Hill to Uxbridge opened in 1904, Ruislip was its only intermediate stop.

name: Ruislip Gardens
fact: Trains had been running past this spot since 1906, but no station was built here until 1934.

name: Ruislip Manor
fact: Passenger numbers here rose from 17,000 in 1931 to 1.25 million in 1937 as the suburb around the station was built.

name: Russell Square
fact: The station has no escalators, so the alternative to its lifts is a spiral staircase of 176 steps.

name: Seven Kings
fact: The platforms are too short for the Elizabeth line's nine-carriage trains, so one carriage's doors are kept shut.

name: Seven Sisters
fact: The name comes from seven elm trees planted in a circle around a walnut tree on Page Green, known as the Seven Sisters by 1732.

name: Shadwell
fact: The station was shut from 1995 to 1998 while the Thames Tunnel its trains run through was repaired.

name: Shenfield
fact: The station opened in 1843, closed in 1850 because too few people used it, and did not reopen until 1887.

name: Shepherd's Bush
fact: It was the original western terminus of the Central London Railway when the line opened in 1900.

name: Shepherd's Bush Market
fact: It was called simply Shepherd's Bush until 2008, when it was renamed to avoid confusion with the other nearby station of that name.

name: Shoreditch High Street
fact: The station is sealed inside a concrete box raised on supports, so that the site around and above it can be built over later.

name: Silver Street
fact: In the 1990s the Fore Street tunnel of the North Circular Road was built directly beneath the station without any disruption to services.

name: Sloane Square
fact: The River Westbourne is carried straight over the platforms in a large iron pipe, still slung from girders above the tracks.

name: Slough
fact: The arrival of the railway here led to Queen Victoria's first ever train journey, from Slough towards Paddington in 1842.

name: Snaresbrook
fact: Opened by the Eastern Counties Railway in 1856, it keeps its Victorian brick building and cast iron and timber platform canopies.

name: South Acton
fact: Until 1959 the station was also served by London Underground District line trains, on a short branch from Acton Town.

name: South Ealing
fact: The station opened on the District Railway in 1883, but District line trains were withdrawn in 1964, leaving only the Piccadilly line.

name: South Hampstead
fact: The station opened in 1879 as Loudon Road and did not take its present name until 1922.

name: South Harrow
fact: In 1903 the line here became the first stretch of the Underground's surface railways to run electric trains instead of steam.

name: South Kensington
fact: It is the busiest station on the whole Underground without step-free access.

name: South Kenton
fact: It is one of only three stations served by London Underground that has no ticket gates at all.

name: South Quay
fact: The whole station was rebuilt 125 metres to the east in 2009, because sharp curves made the old one impossible to lengthen.

name: South Ruislip
fact: The frieze of concrete, glass and granite chippings in the booking hall is one of the earliest public works by the glass artist Henry Haig.

name: South Tottenham
fact: The station opened in 1871 as South Tottenham and Stamford Hill, and only lost the second half of its name in 1949.

name: South Wimbledon
fact: On the original plans the station was going to be called Merton Grove.

name: South Woodford
fact: The station was called George Lane until 1937, then South Woodford (George Lane) until the brackets were dropped in 1947.

name: Southall
fact: The platform signs give the station's name in Gurmukhi script as well as English, reflecting the area's Punjabi community.

name: Southbury
fact: The station opened as Churchbury in 1891, closed twice, and only reopened under its present name in 1960.

name: Southfields
fact: During the Wimbledon Championships more than three times the usual number of passengers pass through the station.

name: Southgate
fact: Charles Holden's station is topped by an illuminated feature designed to look as though it came from Frankenstein's laboratory.

name: Southwark
fact: One wall of the station is made from 660 specially cut pieces of blue glass, designed by the artist Alexander Beleschenko.

name: St James Street
fact: A separate staircase once let passengers reach the platform without entering the station, until it was closed in 2015 to enforce ticket barriers.

name: St. James's Park
fact: The station sits inside 55 Broadway, the old Underground headquarters, which carries carvings by Jacob Epstein, Eric Gill and Henry Moore.

name: St. John's Wood
fact: It is the only Underground station whose name contains none of the letters in the word mackerel.

name: St. Paul's
fact: The station opened in 1900 under the name Post Office, and only became St. Paul's in 1937.

name: Stamford Brook
fact: In 1964 it became the first station anywhere on the Underground to be fitted with an automatic ticket barrier.

name: Stamford Hill
fact: The ticket hall stands in the London Borough of Hackney, but much of the platform area is in Haringey.

name: Stanmore
fact: When it opened, the Metropolitan Railway's trains here competed with a rival service from Stanmore Village station about a kilometre away.

name: Star Lane
fact: The station stands on the route of the Eastern Counties and Thames Junction Railway, open between Stratford and Canning Town since 1846.

name: Stepney Green
fact: The leftmost bay of the 1902 street frontage was a parcel office, bombed and demolished during the Second World War.

name: Stockwell
fact: It opened in 1890 as the southern terminus of the City and South London Railway, London's first successful deep-level tube.

name: Stoke Newington
fact: The station opened in 1872 but only appeared on the Tube map in 2015, when London Overground took it over.

name: Stonebridge Park
fact: The original station was destroyed by bombing in the Second World War, and the buildings standing today date from 1948.

name: Stratford
fact: With 19 platforms, it is the busiest station on the London Underground network outside Zone 1.

name: Stratford High Street
fact: A station here closed in 1957 for lack of passengers, and the site went 54 years without one until the DLR arrived in 2011.

name: Stratford International
fact: Despite the name, no international services have ever called here: the planned Eurostar stops never happened.

name: Sudbury Hill
fact: Charles Holden's brick, concrete and glass station building was made a Grade II listed building in 1994.

name: Sudbury Town
fact: Charles Holden's brick box of a station, capped with a flat concrete slab roof, is a Grade II* listed building.

name: Surrey Quays
fact: The station opened in 1869 as Deptford Road, became Surrey Docks in 1911, and was renamed again in 1989 after a shopping centre.

name: Swiss Cottage
fact: The station is named after a nearby pub built in 1803, originally called The Swiss Tavern.

name: Sydenham
fact: The railway here runs along the bed of the Croydon Canal, which in 1836 became the first canal abandoned by an Act of Parliament.

name: Taplow
fact: The station is unusually large and grand for the number of people it serves because several major Great Western Railway shareholders lived nearby.

name: Temple
fact: Local property owners insisted the station building stay a single storey, and its roof is now an open-air gallery called The Artist's Garden.

name: Theobalds Grove
fact: Named after the grounds of Theobalds Palace, the station closed twice, in 1909 and 1919, before reopening for good in 1960.

name: Theydon Bois
fact: The station opened in April 1865 as plain Theydon and only gained the Bois part of its name that December.

name: Tooting Bec
fact: Designed by Charles Holden, the station was called Trinity Road (Tooting Bec) until 1950 and is now Grade II listed.

name: Tooting Broadway
fact: The station was Charles Holden's first major project for the Underground, fronted by a double-height curving screen of white Portland stone.

name: Tottenham Court Road
fact: The Northern line platforms opened in 1907 as Oxford Street station, while the station now called Goodge Street was then Tottenham Court Road.

name: Tottenham Hale
fact: Until 1868 cattle from East Anglia were unloaded here and driven on foot towards London down what is now the A10.

name: Totteridge & Whetstone
fact: Opened in 1872, the station spent nearly 70 years as a main-line stop before the Northern line took it over in 1940.

name: Tower Gateway
fact: The DLR's original terminus was built on the site of a vanished railway station called Minories.

name: Tower Hill
fact: A section of the Roman city wall is visible above the track at the far eastern end of the westbound platform.

name: Tufnell Park
fact: The station has lifts rather than escalators, and its southbound platform sits at a lower level than the northbound one.

name: Turkey Street
fact: The station opened in 1891 as Forty Hill and only took the name Turkey Street when it reopened in 1960.

name: Turnham Green
fact: Piccadilly line trains only stop here early in the morning and after 22:30, running straight through for the rest of the day.

name: Turnpike Lane
fact: Charles Holden gave the station a huge brick ticket hall half-sunk into the ground; the names North Harringay and Ducketts Green were considered first.

name: Twyford
fact: For nine months from 1839 this was the end of the Great Western Railway, while Sonning Cutting was still being dug.

name: Upminster
fact: The easternmost station on the Underground network, its Victorian platform buildings were originally designed for Hornchurch.

name: Upminster Bridge
fact: The ticket hall floor is tiled with a reversed swastika, a popular decorative pattern at the time the station was built.

name: Upney
fact: The station opened in 1932 to serve the vast new Becontree estate and takes its name from Upney Lane in Barking.

name: Upper Holloway
fact: The line through here opened in 1868 but did so badly that services stopped completely in January 1870 and had to be revived.

name: Upton Park
fact: It was the first station on the London, Tilbury and Southend Railway built by a property developer, who was also building the housing estate around it.

name: Uxbridge
fact: Charles Holden's 1938 station has stained glass by Erwin Bossanyi and stone winged wheels by Joseph Armitage above the entrance.

name: Vauxhall
fact: A popular theory holds that the Russian word for a railway station, vokzal, comes from the name Vauxhall.

name: Victoria
fact: Victoria has seen more visits from royalty and heads of state than any other London station, and the Unknown Warrior arrived here in 1920.

name: Walthamstow Central
fact: It is the nearest station to Walthamstow Market, the longest outdoor market in Europe.

name: Walthamstow Queens Road
fact: The station was simply called Walthamstow when it opened in 1894 and only gained the Queen's Road part of its name in 1968.

name: Wandsworth Road
fact: The station opened in 1863 on the London, Chatham and Dover Railway, whose line through it closed in 1916.

name: Wanstead
fact: The unfinished tunnels east of the station were used as a secret Plessey munitions factory between 1942 and 1945.

name: Wanstead Park
fact: Despite the name, the station is in Forest Gate and stands near Wanstead Flats rather than Wanstead Park.

name: Wapping
fact: The station sits at the north end of Marc Brunel's Thames Tunnel, and passengers reach the platforms through one of its original access shafts.

name: Warren Street
fact: The Victoria line platforms were originally tiled with a maze, a visual pun on the word warren.

name: Warwick Avenue
fact: The station has no building at street level and was one of the first on the Underground designed for escalators rather than lifts.

name: Waterloo
fact: The London Necropolis Company ran a private funeral station inside Waterloo, carrying coffins and mourners to Brookwood Cemetery.

name: Watford
fact: The Metropolitan Railway meant to push on into the town centre but never did, leaving the station about a mile from Watford High Street.

name: Watford High Street
fact: Bakerloo line trains called here from 1917 until the Underground service was withdrawn in September 1982.

name: Watford Junction
fact: The phrase north of Watford is said to come from this station being the last urban stop on the main line out of London.

name: Wembley Central
fact: The station opened in 1842 as Sudbury and went through three more names before settling on Wembley Central in 1948.

name: Wembley Park
fact: The station was built to serve Watkin's Tower, a 1,200ft rival to the Eiffel Tower that was never finished and was demolished in 1904.

name: West Acton
fact: A Grade II listed building by Great Western Railway architect Brian Lewis, it is the only intermediate stop on the Ealing Broadway branch.

name: West Brompton
fact: The main line platforms closed in 1940 and did not reopen until 1999, when transport minister Glenda Jackson did the honours.

name: West Croydon
fact: The station opened as plain Croydon in 1839 and was only renamed West Croydon in 1851.

name: West Drayton
fact: District Railway trains from Mansion House called here on their way to Windsor between 1883 and 1885, until the service was dropped as uneconomic.

name: West Ealing
fact: The station opened in 1871 as Castle Hill, became Castle Hill Ealing Dean in 1875, and only took the name West Ealing in 1899.

name: West Finchley
fact: The station's footbridge is said to have been brought here second-hand from a Yorkshire colliery railway that closed in 1930.

name: West Ham
fact: The station was built at the request of Arnold Hills, whose Thames Ironworks football team went on to become West Ham United.

name: West Hampstead
fact: Metropolitan line trains rush past on their own tracks either side of the Jubilee line platforms without stopping.

name: West Harrow
fact: Trains ran past the site for nine years before the station opened in 1913, and one of its entrances still has no ticket barriers.

name: West India Quay
fact: Just 199 metres separate it from Canary Wharf DLR, the shortest gap between any two stations on the Underground and DLR network.

name: West Kensington
fact: The station opened in 1874 as North End (Fulham) and, despite its name, stands in Hammersmith and Fulham rather than Kensington.

name: West Ruislip
fact: The Central line was meant to carry on westwards from here, with the next station at Harefield Road, until the Green Belt stopped it.

name: West Silvertown
fact: The station opened in 2005 on the DLR's branch to King George V, built to serve Britannia Village.

name: Westbourne Park
fact: A bomb planted by suffragettes was discovered at the station on 16 May 1913.

name: Westferry
fact: The station is named after Westferry Road, but there was never a west ferry: the crossing was at the southern tip of the Isle of Dogs.

name: Westminster
fact: Building the Jubilee line here meant digging a 39-metre void next to Big Ben, the deepest excavation ever made in central London.

name: White City
fact: Trains run on the right through the station rather than the left, a legacy of the tunnels built for the old Wood Lane station.

name: White Hart Lane
fact: The station opened on White Hart Lane in 1872, 27 years before the football ground that took its name from the same road.

name: Whitechapel
fact: The Whitechapel Road entrance is the original 1876 East London Railway frontage, a three-storey building unlike any other on that line.

name: Willesden Green
fact: The ticket hall keeps rare original green mosaic tiling from Charles Walter Clark's 1925 rebuild, and the station is Grade II listed.

name: Willesden Junction
fact: Victorians nicknamed it Bewildering Junction because of its maze of entrances, passages and platforms.

name: Wimbledon
fact: An Airedale terrier called Laddie collected over £5,000 for charity at the station and was later stuffed and displayed on the platform.

name: Wimbledon Park
fact: The stretch of line through here was the last part of the District to swap steam trains for electric ones, in August 1905.

name: Wood Green
fact: Charles Holden's 1932 station was nearly called Lordship Lane, and every station from Turnpike Lane to Cockfosters is now listed.

name: Wood Lane
fact: Opened in 2008, it was the first station built on an existing Tube line in more than 70 years.

name: Wood Street
fact: The station opened in 1873 to replace Shern Hall Street when the Chingford line was extended northwards.

name: Woodford
fact: The station opened in 1856, more than 90 years before the Central line took over the branch in 1947.

name: Woodgrange Park
fact: The name comes from the area's medieval role as a grange, or farm estate, belonging to Stratford Langthorne Abbey.

name: Woodside Park
fact: It opened as Torrington Park in 1872, was renamed within a month, and comes last alphabetically among Underground stations.

name: Woolwich
fact: The station was not in the original Crossrail plans and was only added after a housing developer helped fund its £162 million cost.

name: Woolwich Arsenal
fact: DLR trains leave the station heading east, because of the way the tunnel is aligned beneath the River Thames.
